analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act in its entirety, with no replacement.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to eight House committees and never received a markup or floor vote in the entire two-year Congress, despite 39 Republican cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act and its companion 2010 law retroactively, restoring federal health and education law to what it was before 2010. It contains no replacement: the insurance market rules, subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and tax provisions of the ACA would all vanish at once. That means protections for people with preexisting conditions and help paying for coverage would end, while the tax increases the ACA placed on high-income households would be repealed.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households, who would see the ACA's 3.8% tax on investment income and additional Medicare tax erased. Brand-name drug makers, who would no longer have to give the 50% discount on Medicare drugs. Banks, which would regain the government-guaranteed student-lending business that the 2010 law moved to direct federal loans. Healthier people who would no longer subsidize coverage for sicker neighbors through community-rated premiums.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, drug makers, private lenders

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals both the Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, effective as of their 2010 enactment, and restores every provision of law those acts changed or repealed as if they had never passed.
Because the repeal is retroactive in form, it restores the pre-2010 legal landscape wholesale: no subsidies, no market rules, no ACA taxes — whatever existed before 2010 comes back as a unit.

Restoring pre-ACA law would erase the ACA's tax provisions, including the 3.8% net investment income tax and the additional Medicare tax on high earners — a tax cut concentrated at the top of the income scale.

Repealing the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act would revive the bank-based federal student lending system (FFEL) that the 2010 law ended in favor of direct federal loans, returning a guaranteed origination role to private lenders.

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions, who under pre-ACA rules could again be denied coverage or charged unaffordable premiums. Low- and middle-income households losing premium tax credits and cost-sharing help. Medicaid expansion enrollees. Seniors paying more for prescription drugs as the Medicare coverage-gap discount disappears. Hospitals, which would absorb more uncompensated care from the newly uninsured.
analysis.who_pays_short: People with preexisting conditions and subsidy recipients

drawbacks.text: The bill is bare repeal with no replacement: it does nothing to preserve coverage for anyone currently insured through the ACA marketplaces, the Medicaid expansion, or the young-adult and preexisting-condition provisions.

Because the repeal restores the law as it stood before 2010, insurers could again deny coverage or set unaffordable premiums based on health status, and the premium tax credits that make marketplace coverage affordable would disappear with no transition.

An honest supporter of repeal would acknowledge that this bill offers no answer for what happens to the tens of millions of people covered through the ACA's mechanisms on the day repeal takes effect — it simply returns to the pre-2010 status quo.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains flow to concentrated interests — a large tax cut for high-income households, restored discounts removed from drug makers, and a revived federal guarantee for bank student lending — while the costs fall broadly on people who get coverage, subsidies, or protections through the ACA. Even readers sympathetic to repealing parts of the ACA would note that this bill does not attempt a transition or replacement; it is a full, immediate erasure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to eight House committees on the day it was introduced, then sent to three subcommittees in early 2017, and it never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 3, 2017, the opening day of the 115th Congress, and referred the same day to eight committees: Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, the Judiciary, House Administration, Rules, and Appropriations.

In January and February 2017 it was referred to subcommittees, including the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Natural Resources Subcommittee on Indian, Insular and Alaska Native Affairs.
That is the entire recorded action history: no committee reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who rely on the ACA for coverage, subsidies, and preexisting-condition protections are better off because the bill never advanced; health insurers, hospitals, and subsidy recipients kept the status quo. The concentrated interests that would have gained — high-income households getting a tax cut, drug makers, and banks — lost the opportunity.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: ACA beneficiaries and people with preexisting conditions

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill on the first day of the 115th Congress and recruited original cosponsors.

for.name: 39 of 241 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 39 cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled this bill for committee action or a floor vote, even with Republicans controlling the House, and pursued a separate partial-repeal health bill instead.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Republican — 39 Republican cosponsors, zero Democrats — and no vote ever occurred that would have tested broader support.

industries.note: Repeal erases the ACA's 3.8% net investment income tax and additional Medicare tax, a tax cut concentrated at the top of the income distribution. The revenue those taxes raised helped fund the coverage subsidies that would also vanish.
Repeal ends the 50% discount manufacturers must give on brand-name drugs for seniors in the Medicare coverage gap, meaning seniors and Medicare pay more for the same drugs.
Repealing the 2010 reconciliation act revives the bank-based FFEL program, restoring a government-guaranteed origination role for private lenders that direct federal loans replaced.

Repeal takes away the subsidized customers, individual mandate, and risk-pool rules that support the individual market, but restores insurers' ability to deny or surcharge people with preexisting conditions and drops the medical loss ratio rules.
Repeal would strip coverage from millions of people, shifting costs to hospitals as uncompensated care — hospitals' financial interest here runs alongside patients' interest in keeping coverage.
Repeal ends the employer mandate penalties, relieving large employers of a requirement tied to whether they offer affordable coverage to workers.
